title: 22. Interview: LLM Evaluation: Metrics, Methods, and LLM-as-a-Judge

sections.title: 9. Interview Questions
sections.body:
This section is deliberately the longest — these questions come up constantly.

### A. Conceptual Q&A

**Q**: What are the main limitations of BLEU?
**A**: BLEU captures only surface n-gram overlap, so it penalizes valid paraphrases and rewards exact-word matches even when the meaning is wrong. It ignores semantics, word order beyond n-grams, and is sensitive to tokenization. It also gives no signal for open-ended answers and was designed for translation, so applying it to dialogue or QA is a stretch. Always pair it with a semantic metric or human spot-checks.

**Q**: When does LLM-as-a-judge fail?
**A**: It fails on tasks where the judge model itself is weak — graduate-level science (GPQA-style), niche domain reasoning, math verification, or any task requiring ground truth the judge can't compute. It also fails when bias is unmitigated (position, length, self-preference), when rubrics are vague, and when the judge and judged model are the same family. Finally, it can confidently agree with a confidently wrong answer, producing high inter-call agreement but low accuracy.

**Q**: What is benchmark contamination and why does it matter?
**A**: Contamination means benchmark items leaked into a model's training data, so the model can score high by memorization rather than reasoning. Symptoms: high benchmark score, poor performance on lightly paraphrased versions, suspiciously perfect recall of exact phrasings. It matters because leaderboard scores stop predicting real-world capability, and consumers over-trust contaminated models. Mitigations include dynamic item generation, paraphrase robustness tests, and held-out private eval sets.

**Q**: How is perplexity misused?
**A**: People use perplexity to compare models across different tokenizers — that's invalid because token granularity changes the per-token loss baseline. They also use it to judge output *quality*, but a model can be low-perplexity on fluent nonsense. Finally, perplexity on in-domain text is not the same as competence; a model trained on legal text will have low perplexity on legalese without actually understanding it. Use perplexity only for same-tokenizer model comparison or in-domain OOD detection.

**Q**: BERTScore vs BLEU — when do I prefer which?
**A**: Prefer BLEU when surface form matters (SQL, code, exact-entity extraction, translation where you want literal fidelity) and you need a fast, deterministic, cheap metric. Prefer BERTScore when paraphrase or synonymy is valid and meaning matters more than exact words (summarization, QA, captioning). BERTScore correlates better with humans on those tasks but is slower and depends on the underlying embedding model. A common pattern is to report both: BLEU for surface fidelity, BERTScore for semantic adequacy.

**Q**: What is position bias in LLM-as-a-judge and how do I fix it?
**A**: In pairwise judging, the judge systematically prefers whichever output appears first (or second, depending on the judge model), independent of quality. Fix it by running each pair twice with swapped positions, then either take the majority vote, mark disagreement as a tie, or average scores. For pointwise judging this bias doesn't apply, but you should still spot-check with multiple judge models and report judge-judge agreement. Reporting results without controlling for position bias is a common, embarrassing interview red flag.

**Q**: Intrinsic vs extrinsic evaluation — define and give an example.
**A**: Intrinsic evaluates the output itself against a reference or rubric (e.g., BLEU on a translation, BERTScore on a summary). Extrinsic evaluates whether the output helps a downstream task (e.g., does a summary let a human answer comprehension questions faster, or does a generated SQL query return correct rows from a database). Intrinsic is cheap and automatable; extrinsic is expensive but better predicts business value. Mature teams use intrinsic for fast iteration and extrinsic for release gates.

**Q**: What are the limits of MMLU as an evaluation signal?
**A**: MMLU is multiple-choice, English-centric, and many items are memorizable, so high scores can reflect contamination rather than reasoning. It samples 57 narrow academic subjects, so it underrepresents modern tasks like multi-step reasoning, tool use, and instruction following. The 4-option format also lets lucky guessing inflate scores, and questions with debatable answers are common. Treat MMLU as one weak signal; corroborate with MMLU-Pro, GPQA, and your own golden dataset.

**Q**: What's the difference between offline and online evaluation, and why do you need both?
**A**: Offline eval runs on a fixed golden set pre-deployment, with references and full control; online eval runs on sampled live traffic post-deployment, usually without references. Offline catches capability gaps before shipping; online catches drift, distribution shift, and regressions that offline missed because the golden set didn't cover them. You need both because offline alone can't see the real world, and online alone can't gate a release. The hybrid sweet spot is shadow-mode online eval on pre-release candidates.

**Q**: Why is self-preference bias dangerous, and how would you detect it?
**A**: Self-preference bias means a judge model prefers outputs from its own model family, so GPT-4 judging GPT-3.5 vs Claude may systematically favor the GPT-style answer. It's dangerous because it produces confident, internally-consistent but unfair rankings. Detect it by running the same eval with multiple judge families and measuring agreement; large divergences flag bias. Mitigate by averaging across judges, using a stronger/different judge, or falling back to human ratings on the disputed cases.

### B. Scenario-Based Questions

**Scenario**: Your team's BLEU score on the translation test set jumped 10% after a model swap, but customer support tickets about "weird translations" doubled within two weeks.
**Task**: Explain what's likely going on and what you'd do to diagnose it.
**Sample Answer**: The most likely cause is that the new model produces output that aligns better with the *reference* translations' surface form (boosting BLEU) but is actually less natural or contextually appropriate for real user inputs. BLEU rewards exact n-gram overlap, so a more literal, stiffer translator can score higher while feeling worse to users. I'd start by clustering the support tickets by error type to find the failure mode, then sample 50-100 of those real inputs and run side-by-side human evaluation between old and new model. I'd also compute BERTScore and run an LLM-judge on fluency and adequacy. If the new model wins on BLEU but loses on human + BERTScore + judge, that confirms BLEU is misleading here and I'd revert or retrain against a richer metric.

**Scenario**: You must pick exactly ONE metric to gate releases for a customer-support chatbot that answers billing questions from a knowledge base.
**Task**: Which metric do you pick and why?
**Sample Answer**: I'd pick **faithfulness via LLM-as-judge** — specifically, whether the answer is fully supported by the retrieved knowledge-base passage. Billing answers must be *correct* (no invented amounts or policies), so surface metrics like BLEU are useless and even BERTScore won't catch a fluent hallucination. A pointwise LLM-judge with a strict faithfulness rubric ("every claim must be traceable to the context; otherwise score <= 2") catches the highest-risk failure. I'd still pair it with a small human audit on a rolling sample for rubric drift, plus an online metric (thumbs-up rate) post-release. If forced to a single number, faithfulness-judge is the one that maps directly to business risk.

**Scenario**: You're building a pairwise LLM-as-judge pipeline and notice that when you swap the order of A and B, the winner flips 30% of the time.
**Task**: What's happening, and what do you do?
**Sample Answer**: That's textbook position bias — the judge's preference depends on which output it sees first, independent of quality. A 30% flip rate is high and means any single-order result is unreliable. First, I'd make the pipeline always run each pair in both orders and report four outcomes: A wins both, B wins both, A-then-B tie, or flip. Only "wins both" counts as a confident win; flips should be marked as ties or excluded. Second, I'd try a different judge model to see if the bias shrinks — some judge models are far worse than others. Third, I'd add a reference if available (reference-based pairwise is much more stable). I'd also log the flip rate itself as a meta-metric, because a rising flip rate over time signals judge degradation.

**Scenario**: Engineering wants to ship a new prompt template that improves average response length by 40% and the LLM-judge score went up accordingly. The product manager is suspicious.
**Task**: How do you determine if the improvement is real?
**Sample Answer**: The PM is right to be suspicious — length bias is one of the best-documented LLM-judge biases, where longer outputs are systematically rated higher. I'd first compute the correlation between output length and judge score across the eval set; if it's high (e.g., r > 0.5), the gain is largely a length artifact. Then I'd run two controls: (1) re-judge with an explicit length-controlled rubric that penalizes verbosity, and (2) force both old and new prompts to produce similar-length outputs (e.g., via max_tokens or a "be concise" instruction) and re-compare. I'd also compute a length-normalized BERTScore and a faithfulness score, which are less length-sensitive. If the improvement survives all three controls, it's likely real; if it collapses, the win was verbosity, not quality.

**Scenario**: Your legal-research product ships a RAG chatbot. Lawyers report that 5% of answers cite nonexistent case law. Leadership asks, "Why didn't our eval catch this?"
**Task**: Diagnose the eval gap and propose a fix.
**Sample Answer**: The likely gap is that the eval was using semantic similarity (BERTScore) or a generic LLM-judge rubric focused on "helpfulness," neither of which verifies that cited entities actually exist. Hallucinated citations look fluent and on-topic, so they pass those metrics. The fix is a **verifiability check** in the eval pipeline: every citation must (a) appear in the retrieved context, and (b) ideally be checked against an external case-law database or the source corpus. Concretely, I'd add a regex/JSON-extraction step that pulls citations from the answer, then asserts each one is present in the retrieved passages — failing the example if any citation is ungrounded. I'd also add a "citation faithfulness" LLM-judge rubric specifically asking whether each cited case is actually supported. This becomes a hard gate before release. I'd additionally sample 100 historical examples where citations were verified and add them to the golden set so this regressions is caught going forward.
